doc.title: Bobby Watson interviewed by Michael Woods, Clinton, New York, January 19, 1996

title: How Watson writes: four bars of inspiration
summary: He explains manipulating notes to move emotions, keeping a journal, and stretching four bars of inspiration into a song through craft.

story.theme_name: Writing and arranging: how musicians compose
story.community_name: Writing, arranging and composing: how the music gets made

blocks.x: to give pride. Or boredom is like [scats]. Like that you know? And so you’d have to guess, and depending on the value of the notes and how hard you hit the notes, you find that those are your tools in composition. That you manipulate the notes and then by doing that you manipulate people’s emotions. And it’s a very exciting thing. So that’s how I write now. Sometimes the chords come first, but most of the time I go for the melody. And I keep a little journal if I hear something I’ll write it down and then I’ll get back to it later. You may change a note here or there, but basically you know, if something comes to you, you write that down. You used to say like your Divine Inspiration — Divine Inspiration doesn’t come that often. And usually when it does it comes in four bars. Very rarely do you hear a song and it’s complete. I must have written a few songs that way, it just comes so fast you can’t hardly get it down on paper, the whole song. I can probably count that on one hand. But most of my songs, you know you have to toil over them, and I get maybe four bars of Divine Inspiration. And with the craft you stretch that into a whole song.
So four bars of inspiration and the rest of the tune of perspiration.

That’s right. There’s only one person wrote in pen and that was Mozart. Everybody else uses pencil you know? So I have to realize that. You know Beethoven, he used a pencil. So I say hey, you know you write it, you throw it away, and you have to, it’s perspiring.
